#4563. Comparison Test: 2027 BMW iX3 vs. Mercedes-Benz GLC400

Their mission is similar, but these two new electric SUVs diverge in their approach to driving and cabin tech.

Wow, a comparison between a BMW and a Mercedes-Benz! Car and Driver is really digging deep into the annals of obscurity with this pairing, eh? While comparing these two German marques is already as popular as a Quarter Pounder with Cheese, there is a fun twist this time around: They’re both electric!

These Teutonic stalwarts are entering brave new territory. The BMW iX3 is the first EV from the Neue Klasse platform, which will also underpin the upcoming i3 sedan. The GLC400 also rides on a new platform, and Mercedes is keen to apply the learnings from the EQXX concept and the CLA-class EV to a larger segment. But which is the better car? Keep reading and find out. (Or spoil it for yourself and scroll to the end. We can’t tell you what to do.)

Right now, both electric SUVs offer just one powertrain, although more variants are soon to come. Their base prices are closely matched, with the BMW starting at $62,850 and the Merc at $64,950. However, options vastly expanded the price delta.

See all results for new 2027 BMW iX3 for sale near 07094

At $75,050, our iX3 50 xDrive had several different option packages, including $4000 to look cooler and pack on more safety tech (the M Sport Professional package); $2500 for traffic-jam and lane-change assists; $1500 for multi-function seats, a panoramic sunroof, and a heated steering wheel; $1200 for a HUD and Harman/Kardon audio; and $750 to make parking easier. A special coat of paint ($650) topped things off.

The GLC400 was even dearer. Our test example carried the $6800 Pinnacle Plus trim, which adds all sorts of fancy features and digital baubles. Another $3950 went toward upgraded driver aids. The Agility & Comfort package, which we’ll bring up later, cost $2900. Various AMG Line aesthetic bits were $3850. Beyond that, there was $1100 for upgraded wheels and $350 for a faux-leather vinyl dashboard. The total rang in at $84,975.

There is no doubt among our logbook commenters that the BMW iX3 is the more futuristic of the two vehicles, inside and out. The Bimmer’s exterior rights the wrongs of the somewhat awkward gas-powered X3, which didn’t get the full Neue Klasse treatment. This thing looks sharp from the outside, with correctly proportional kidney grilles, a slickly integrated headlight array, and a squarish body with a bit of drama around the fenders. The GLC design takes more of an evolutionary approach; the overall silhouette is largely the same despite its new platform and larger dimensions, but the new taillight arrangement spices things up a bit. And then there’s the massive silver grille, which stands out in all the wrong ways against contrasting body colors.

The interiors drew more polarized opinions. The BMW iX3 has the weirder of the two cabins by far. The primary infotainment touchscreen is huge, high-resolution, and shaped like a parallelogram for some reason. Above that lives a dash-spanning strip that acts as the instrument cluster, putting the most pertinent information at eye level, while allowing for additional features to be displayed closer to the passenger. About half the staff liked it, and the other half (dare we say it, the half that trends older) found it unnecessarily odd. Thankfully, it’s easy to work with over time and is sufficiently customizable. What’s truly gratuitous, though, is that a HUD is available. All that info is right there at eye level already! Save yourself the $1200. Nobody really liked the steering wheel design either.

See all results for new 2027 BMW iX3 for sale near 07094

Whereas BMW’s interior drew about a 50/50 blend of love and hate, the GLC400’s interior accrued vastly more derision. The optional A-pillar-to-A-pillar Hyperscreen came in for the most criticism, in part because its flat surface picks up and highlights fingerprints way too easily, and in part because it’s simply too much damn screen. Did Mercedes even need to hire a dashboard designer? Because the dash is largely screen. Thankfully, the system’s bones have been kicking around long enough through various iterations that this setup is dummy-simple to master. Editors also dinged the GLC400 for plasticky trim not befitting the car’s price. But hey, at least these vents are manually adjustable; can’t say the same for the iX3.

Both electric SUVs here have dual-motor, all-wheel-drive layouts. The iX3 50 xDrive makes 463 horsepower and 476 pound-feet of torque, while the GLC400 has a bit more vim at 483 horses and 590 pound-feet, as well as a two-speed gearbox on its rear motor to improve high-speed efficiency. But the Merc’s extra power must contend with extra mass; the GLC400 weighs in at 5605 pounds on our scales against the comparatively svelte 5186-pound iX3.

HIGHS: Corner-carving dynamics, cool futuristic looks, fabulous pedal feel.LOWS: Crashy over imperfect roads, polarizing infotainment layout, wholly unnecessary HUD.VERDICT: It’d be our choice if we lived on the Nürburgring.

The GLC400’s extra muscle overcomes the extra mass, and the Mercedes wins the acceleration crown, hustling to 60 mph in 3.7 seconds and reaching the quarter-mile in 12.2 seconds at 114 mph. That’s just a bit ahead of the BMW, which needs 4.3 seconds to hit 60 and crosses the quarter-mile mark in 12.7 seconds at 113 mph. The GLC400 is also quicker from 5 to 60 mph, and from 30 to 50, while the iX3 snags top honors in the 50–70 sprint.

The two vehicles are nearly evenly matched in braking. The GLC400 needs just 160 feet to clamp down from 70 mph, and the iX3 needs 163. The story is the same from 100 mph, where the Merc requires 322 feet, and the BMW asks for 328. The two are also nearly identical around the skidpad: 0.87 g for Mercedes, 0.88 g for BMW.

We saw even greater parity in our 75-mph real-world highway range tests, with both EVs tied at 330 miles of range. That’s a great showing for the Merc, which carries an EPA range estimate of 350 miles; it’s less so for the BMW, which on its 22-inch wheels is EPA estimated at 392 miles. We found further similarities in charging the batteries; both averaged above 180 kilowatts over the course of the fill-up, with the iX3 peaking at 389 kilowatts and the GLC400 topping out at 350 kilowatts.

The topic of driving dynamics is where the logbook comments truly diverged. With few exceptions, our editors were not over the moon about the tuning of the iX3’s coil springs and passive dampers. Riding on 22-inch wheels, the BMW felt way too stiff around our rural Michigan evaluation loop. On the smoother pavement, the Bimmer felt fine, but there was vastly more head toss and bounce when careening over the bumpier stuff. And many editors felt the steering was too numb.

That said, there was no shortage of praise for the iX3’s acceleration and braking. The BMW’s pedal response inspired more confidence than in the Mercedes. And if you love e-noises, the BMW’s sound synthesizer is definitely on the wackier side of the EV soundscape—which we suppose makes sense, given the BMW’s vastly more futuristic vibe overall.

HIGHS: Excellent highway range, luxurious ride with more composure on demand, quiet cabin.LOWS: Not-so-super Hyperscreen, some wallow on glassy roads, expensive options list.VERDICT: Our preferred all-rounder.

The GLC400, on the other hand, received far more praise for its ride and handling balance. It’s not the best-riding SUV in its class—one editor contends the Volvo EX60 claims that title—but it’s definitely up there. To be fair, most of this comes down to the aforementioned $2900 Agility & Comfort package, which adds air springs, adaptive dampers, and rear-axle steering. The ride is vastly smoother over bad pavement, though on the smooth stuff, it can feel just a smidge too soft, like you’re driving atop pudding.

You can reinstate some composure in the GLC by switching to Sport mode, which stiffens things up, albeit just enough to eat away the too-soft portion of the suspension tuning. The GLC’s interior features better sound isolation—to the tune of 1 decibel (3 sones) at 70 mph—and what bump sounds do make their way out of the wheel wells barely infiltrate the cabin.

When really chucking both cars around, the BMW may eke out a small advantage in driving enjoyment, but that’s not the most common use case for a compact electric SUV. When it comes to the brass tacks of daily life—your commute, your soccer-practice runs, your bleary-eyed late-night amble to the grocery store—the GLC400 is the superior craft. The BMW’s minor advantage in spirited driving does not overcome the fact that the GLC, as equipped here, has a greater advantage where it counts the most every day. Provided you spec the Agility & Comfort package, the GLC400 feels like the wiser choice to us.

#4562. The 2027 Kia EV6 is over $8,000 more than the new EV3

Kia announced that 2027 EV6 prices start at about $38,000, or $8,000 more than the new EV3.

The 2027 Kia EV6 arrives as a carryover model from last year. After reducing prices on the 2026 model year by $5,000 just a few months ago, the 2027 EV6 remains the same price across all trims.

The base EV6 Light standard-range RWD model starts at $37,900, not including the $1,545 destination fee, which is the same as last year.

Powered by a 63 kWh battery, the standard-range variant offers up to 237 miles of range. Upgrading to the EV6 Light long range RWD model costs an extra $3,300, starting at $41,200, but delivers up to 319 miles of range using a larger 84 kWh battery.

The 84 kWh battery offers up to 319 miles of range in RWD variants, while AWD EV6 models get up to 295 miles. The top-spec EV6 GT-Line AWD has up to 270 miles of range.

Kia said that with the EV6 MSRP unchanged and the launch of the new EV3, it’s “making EVs more attainable for those who embrace the fully electric lifestyle.”

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at just $29,890, or about $8,000 less than the EV6. Kia’s entry-level electric SUV is available in five trims: Light, Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT.

The lowest-priced EV3 Light FWD model uses a 58.3 kWh battery and delivers an EPA-estimated range of up to 221 miles.

Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT, use a larger 81.4 kWh battery that delivers up to 321 miles of range on a single charge. Like the EV6, the EV3 is also available with front-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive powertrain options.

Inside, both the EV6 and EV3 feature Kia’s ccNC infotainment system. The setup includes nearly 30″ of screen space in a curved panoramic display, including dual 12.3″ instrument cluster and central navigation screens, plus a 5″ climate control touchscreen.

Both also include a native NACS port so that you can access Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter.

However, the EV6 uses an 800V architecture, enabling faster charging than the EV3, which uses a 400V system.

I've had four EVs and the 800v charging system on my 2025 Ioniq 5 is the biggest improvement I have experienced in any EV. My road trip stops are now about 20 minutes to go from 15% to 85% at fast chargers. To me, this is a game changer. When people talk about range anxiety, they are really talking about long recharging times and with these speeds, you'll be back on the road in the time it takes to hit the restroom and grab a bit to eat.

The EV6 can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes, whereas the EV3 takes about 30 minutes.

The EV6 is also larger and less boxy than the EV3, measuring 184.8″ long, 74″ wide, and 60.8″ tall, with a 114.2″ wheelbase. In comparison, the EV3 is 169.3″ long, 72.8″ wide, and 62″ tall, with a 105.5″ wheelbase.

Which one would you drive? The new EV3, the EV6, or would you go with Kia’s three-row EV9? Let us know in the comments.

With the new 2027 models arriving, Kia is offering a $10,000 customer cash discount on the 2026 EV9, $5,000 on the 2026 EV6, and $1,500 on the 2027 EV3 to clear inventory. You can use the links below to see what’s available near you.

#4561. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

#4560. VW’s EV Factory Is Now Taking Cars Apart. There’s Money In It

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volkswagen has spent years converting its Zwickau factory to build electric cars, and now only electric cars roll off its production lines. But now it has received a new assignment: taking cars apart. The German plant has opened an industrial dismantling line, adding a new revenue stream.

Zwickau became VW’s electric manufacturing hub through a €1.2 billion conversion that began in 2018. ID.3 production started in November 2019, the last combustion car followed in June 2020, and the transformation was completed in January 2022 with the ID.5. Retooled production lines, extra automation, and extensive employee training now enable the factory to build six MEB-based EVs for Volkswagen, Audi, and Cupra.

The new eight-stage dismantling line will initially handle preproduction vehicles, but will eventually also handle cars at the end of their life. From 2027, it will process 4,100 vehicles annually across two shifts, employing 100 workers who were retrained for the new role. Construction and approvals took nine months, finishing three months early; VW says it could reuse manufacturing equipment to cut costs.

The automaker says it has been selling usable original parts recovered at Zwickau since July, with doors, bumpers, motors and transmission components reportedly in especially high demand. They’re available through its dealer and service networks, independent workshops and parts retailers.

The idea is to make repairs affordable enough to keep older cars on the road instead of writing them off. The dismantling line initially handles pre-production vehicles, although VW doesn’t identify which cars supplied the parts already sold. It also hasn’t disclosed prices, sales volumes, warranty terms, or how it inspects components before resale.

Material recovery is another money-making opportunity. Separating plastics before recycling helps preserve their usefulness for new components. VW says plastic recovered from one vehicle could contribute recycled material to three new cars (not all of it, though).

VW is also looking to expand its recycling business and plans to invest up to €90 million, with the Saxony government pledging €10.7 million, and it could eventually support 1,000 jobs. Zwickau has no vehicle production planned beyond 2031, though, so this new recycling line still leaves its long-term future uncertain.

That uncertainty comes as Volkswagen’s rising EV sales are putting pressure on its profit margins, because its electric models still earn less than combustion cars. The squeeze has also prompted it to pause development of the upcoming electric Golf until it can accommodate the investment. For now, dismantling remains a business whose profitability at scale needs proving, and it’s unclear if this can generate enough work (and profit) to really matter for the Zwickau plant.

VW hasn't said the operation will be limited to EVs, though, and the photos it published seem to suggest otherwise. At least one of the cars pictured (the dark blue one) appears to be a Golf, although the captions don’t identify the models. Zwickau may build only electric cars, but its new used parts business looks set to cater to a broader crowd to maximize revenue potential.

#4559. The Bestselling Luxury Vehicles of 2026

Which models from the likes of BMW, Mercedes, and Lexus are the biggest hitters on the sales charts? We've gathered the numbers and ranked the top 10 sellers.

You're surely already familiar with the bestselling vehicles in America overall—Ford F-150s and Honda CR-Vs are everywhere on our roads and regularly dominate the sales charts. But what about vehicles with a bit more prestige? We've gathered the numbers for luxury-badged vehicles to see which models are selling the best so far in 2026, and while some are the usual suspects, other entries here may be more popular than you realize. Of course, they're all SUVs, but what else would you expect? We’ve now updated this list with sales numbers through the first three quarters of 2026.

More Sales Charts: Bestselling Cars in 2026 | Bestselling EVs in 2026 | Bestselling Luxury Cars in 2025

It would take a lot for any other luxury vehicle to dethrone the Lexus RX from atop the charts, as this model has been a top seller for decades now. The RX isn't exactly a standout in any one area, but it has a well-established reputation as a comfortable luxury SUV and it does many things well. There are also multiple hybrid powertrains available to broaden its appeal.

The outgoing X5 was one of the oldest models in BMW's lineup, and it's being replaced by a new generation for 2027 (pictured). This changeover didn't stop the X5 from being the brand's bestselling model, however, with sales up nearly 24 percent through the first three quarters.

Mercedes-Benz GLE-Class: 60,253 units sold

The GLE is Mercedes-Benz's mid-size SUV; the "E" in its name designates it as the equivalent to the E-class sedan. It gets a significant refresh for 2027 (pictured), and is selling well compared with last year. (These figures come from Automotive News, as Mercedes-Benz stopped publicly reporting sales figures by model in 2025.)

The X3 was new for the 2025 model year, and it appears that buyers are sold on the new design. Its sales were up significantly through the first three quarters of this year, although it wasn't quite enough to make this the bestselling BMW.

Mercedes-Benz GLC-Class: 53,986 units sold

The GLC is falling behind in the sales race with its closest competitor, the BMW X3. The BMW has pulled ahead as of late, but we'll see if the arrival of new AMG variants could change that later in the year. (These figures come from Automotive News, as Mercedes-Benz stopped publicly reporting sales figures by model in 2025.)

The NX's tweener size (it fits between the subcompact and compact luxury segments) makes it a popular choice for those looking for a small-ish premium SUV. It’s significantly updated for 2027 and now comes only with hybrid powertrains: the NX350h serves as the base powertrain, while the plug-in hybrid NX450h+ offers more power and a bit of electric range.

Lexus was selling plenty of luxury SUVs long before the TX arrived, but it turns out the brand was correct to split off a separate three-row model. The hot-selling RX briefly offered a three-row variant called the RX L several years ago, but now that the new-ish TX nameplate has established itself, it's racking up a significant number of sales on its own.

Acura was one of the first luxury brands to launch a three-row crossover, and the MDX is still going strong. Its sales were up nearly 25 percent through the first three quarters of this year.

The Q5 compact SUV is Audi's bestseller, and it was new for 2025. Sales are up slightly through the first three quarters of this year, so it managed to sneak back onto this list. The Audi has some work to do to catch up to its biggest rivals, which are selling better.

The current generation of the XC90 has been around for a decade now, but Volvo has kept it fresh with numerous updates, and it's still a strong seller. It's having a good year so far, and it edges out the smaller XC60 to become the bestselling Volvo.

#4558. Lectric launches XP Lite3 e-bike, the new best low-cost model in the US

Lectric eBikes, the largest electric bike company in the US by just about any metric you can measure, has just unveiled its latest model: the Lectric XP Lite3. And with a starting price of just $799, the new lightweight folding electric bike is continuing the company’s tradition of packing surprisingly impressive features into remarkably affordable e-bikes.

The XP Lite2 had been widely considered the best bang-for-your-buck option in the ultra-budget category, offering an affordable yet punchy Class 2 e-bike for a song, despite still coming from a reputable US-based company with strong reputation for warranty and support.

Now, the third-generation model builds on what has become one of the most successful budget e-bike platforms in the country, bringing a long list of upgrades designed to make the bike easier to ride, fold, transport, and live with.

And perhaps most importantly, Lectric has managed to keep that familiar $799 starting price that debuted on the original XP Lite1 all the way back in 2022.

The new Lectric XP Lite3 weighs just 49 lb (22.2 kg), making it one of the lighter options in Lectric’s extensive lineup of folding electric bikes. That’s still no featherweight, partly due to Lectric’s insistence on not neutering the bike’s performance, but it’s still a solid 10-20 lb lighter than the average direct-to-consumer e-bike these days.

The bike retains the compact folding design that made its predecessors popular with everyone from college students to RV owners, but introduces a redesigned frame with improved ergonomics and a reinforced folding latch borrowed from the company’s flagship XP4 model.

New quick-release pedals further reduce the bike’s storage footprint, making it easier to squeeze into a car trunk, apartment closet, or RV storage compartment.

Despite its compact dimensions, the XP Lite3 can support a maximum payload of 275 lb (125 kg) and accommodates riders ranging from 4’8” to 6’2”.

The bike reaches speeds of up to 20 mph (32 km/h) and offers up to 40 miles (64 km) or 80 miles (128 km) of range in Eco mode, though expect significantly less range when using higher-power pedal assist or throttle-only riding. The range discrepancy comes from two different battery offerings. The base model features a 374 Wh battery, while the long-range version has nearly twice the capacity at 672 Wh.

Power comes from Lectric’s Stealth M24 motor, which is rated at 300W continuous but over 800 peak watts. The motor combines with Lectric’s pedal assist selector to offer five levels of pedal assist that are personalizable, letting riders dial in exactly how much boost they’d like on their ride. Riders also get a twist throttle, a more comfortable style of throttle enabled by the lack of shifters crowding the bars on this single-speed e-bike.

Several other upgrades help the XP Lite3 punch above its weight class, including integrated rear turn signals, a bright 3.5-inch full-color display brought over from other recently launched models in the Lectric lineup, and a redesigned LevelUp Lite rear rack with new mounting possibilities.

Stopping power comes from Star Union 602 hydraulic disc brakes with thicker 2.3 mm rotors, another welcome feature on a bike at this price point.

Lectric is also offering a Gates Carbon Belt Drive version of the XP Lite3, giving riders a cleaner, quieter, and virtually maintenance-free alternative to a traditional chain drivetrain. That Gates belt drive model fetches a $100 premium, but is likely worth it for those who value the cleaner, maintenance-free alternative that is likely to outlast the bike itself.

The chain-drive version comes in Arctic White, Blue Mist, Matte Grey, and Matte Lavender, while the belt-drive model is offered in JW Black and Ballerina Pink.

It’s difficult to overstate just how much Lectric has changed the American electric bicycle industry.

The Phoenix, Arizona-based company has grown into the country’s largest e-bike brand by both sales volume and the total number of e-bikes on the road. In doing so, it has become one of the most recognizable names in affordable electric transportation.

But Lectric didn’t get there by simply building cheap electric bikes.

Instead, the company helped revolutionize what consumers should expect from a budget-friendly e-bike, combining capable hardware, practical designs, and aggressive pricing with something that has historically been missing from much of the low-cost e-bike market: a real American company standing behind the product.

While countless inexpensive e-bikes sold online come from little-known overseas brands with questionable long-term support, Lectric has built its reputation around US-based customer service, accessible replacement parts, and a company that riders can actually reach when something goes wrong.

That’s a big part of what has made the XP Lite series so important.

Since its introduction, the XP Lite series has arguably set the standard for what an entry-level electric bike should be. It isn’t necessarily the most powerful, fastest, or fanciest e-bike on the road, but it delivers the essentials at a price that opens electric cycling to an entirely new audience.

And importantly, it does so without requiring riders to gamble on an unknown brand.

The XP Lite3 continues that formula, adding features like hydraulic disc brakes, integrated turn signals, and a color display that would have been difficult to imagine on a $799 e-bike just a few years ago.

I’ve been following Lectric since the company’s earliest days, and it’s been fascinating to watch how the brand has consistently raised the bar for affordable electric bikes. I rode one of Lectric’s first 10 bikes off their nascent production line all the way back in 2019, and I think they’d agree that few people outside the company know the brand better than I do. So I can say that, without a doubt, this is one of the company’s most important launches to date because of how it revolutionizes how much bike someone can get without stretching their budget farther than they have to. And at a time when inflation is still rising unchecked and fuel prices are through the roof, this is what the industry needs more than ever.

Keep in mind that the $799 price tag for the XP Lite3 announced today is the same price that the original XP Lite carried back in 2022, despite that value ballooning to $939 in 2026 dollars due to rising inflation.

What impresses me most isn’t necessarily any single feature on the new XP Lite3. It’s the combination of all those features at a price that remains accessible to so many riders.

Hydraulic brakes, a color display, integrated turn signals, a refined folding mechanism, and even the option for a Gates belt drive? That’s quite a lot of bike for the money. And remember, the performance is still there. This is still a 48V e-bike with a legit 20 mph (32 km/h) top speed on throttle and pedal assist.

Sure, there are lighter e-bikes out there, and there are certainly more premium models with fancier components. But that’s not really the point of the XP Lite.

The point is to make electric biking accessible without making it feel like a compromise at every turn.

And when you consider that you’re getting all of this from the biggest e-bike company in the country, complete with US-based support and a proven track record, it’s hard to argue with the value proposition.

The original XP Lite helped establish what a good affordable electric bike could be. The XP Lite3 looks ready to move that benchmark forward once again.

And on a personal note, not only do I want my own Lectric XP Lite3 now, but I think my wife’s new e-bike will soon be an XP Lite3 in Ballerina Pink with a Gates belt drive. Remember, “Happy wife, happy life!”

#4557. Polestar 2 Production Is Officially Over. A Successor Is Coming In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The first-generation Polestar 2 is dead for good. Production of the brand’s first electric model has ended in Luqiao, China, a company representative confirmed to InsideEVs after a report from Norway’s TV2 surfaced last month.

After six years in production, Polestar’s first mass-market model sold roughly 200,000 units worldwide and set the stage for what came next. The Polestar 2 competed with the Tesla Model 3, and although it was smaller and more expensive than the American-made electric sedan, it had plenty of fans everywhere. (Healthy lease discounts likely helped.)

The European-spec Polestar 2 got its last facelift last year.

The lovable four-door electric sedan went through several facelifts, including one that significantly changed the way it drives. When the car was introduced in 2000, its base trim was front-wheel drive, and dual-motor all-wheel drive was available as an option. But in 2023, the entry-level models became rear-wheel drive, while the top versions continued to offer AWD.

More power and more range were also added along the way, keeping the CMA-based EV up to date in an increasingly crowded market. At its peak, the Polestar 2 had up to 314 miles of EPA-estimated range, which is plenty for daily use, but ultimately the Tesla Model 3’s lower price made the Swedish-designed EV a tougher sell.

In the United States, the Polestar 2 was discontinued last year, a move that seemed to foreshadow the brand’s demise stateside. While the company’s entry-level model was axed because of hiked import tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, Polestar was ultimately strong-armed to stop selling vehicles here, after a decision from the U.S. Department of Commerce denied the automaker an authorization under the Connected Vehicle Rule.

That said, Polestar continues to sell EVs in Europe and other parts of the world, and while the first-generation Polestar 2 has been discontinued globally, a new generation is scheduled to debut next year.

With a design inspired by the Formula 2030 concept, the new Polestar 2 is expected to follow in its predecessor’s footsteps as a mashup between a small sedan and crossover, though the company hasn’t confirmed what lies in store for the new model, design-wise.

The new Polestar 2 is part of the Geely-owned automaker’s plan to launch no fewer than four new models in just three years. Half of that plan has already been enacted, with the Polestar 5 grand tourer and Polestar 4 SUV already going on sale in Europe earlier this year. #4556. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4555. Ford’s new sub-$30K electric truck can power your home for a lot less

Ford wants to make powering your home with an EV a lot cheaper. Its upcoming sub-$30,000 Fathom electric truck will feature a new bidirectional charging system that ditches the need for an expensive external inverter.

Arriving in 2027, the Fathom will be the first EV from a US automaker priced below $30,000 that can deliver more than 10 kW of AC power to a home without a separate wall-mounted inverter.

And Ford says it’s cutting the cost of the other equipment needed for home backup power, too.

EV batteries store electricity as direct current (DC), but our homes use alternating current (AC). To send power from an EV battery into a house, traditionally, that meant installing a pricey external inverter.

Ford has come up with a different approach for its new Universal EV Platform, which will underpin the Fathom.

After acquiring startup Auto Motive Power in 2023, Ford redesigned its bidirectional charging system from the ground up. Instead of relying on a separate wall-mounted inverter, it built one directly into the truck’s E-box, one of the vehicle’s five main modules.

Fewer parts mean lower costs, and Ford says the savings will extend to the home charging equipment, too.

Fathom owners will have two ways to use the truck’s battery to power their homes.

Home Power Management will let owners charge their truck when electricity rates are low, then use that stored power at home when rates are higher. That could mean real savings for households on time-of-use electricity plans. They’ll need Ford’s new Home Power Station, which the company expects to cost about half as much as its first-generation bidirectional charger.

Home Backup Power will let the truck keep the lights on during an outage. For that, owners will need both the Home Power Station and Ford’s Home Backup Panel. Ford says the backup hardware should cost at least 60% less than its first-generation equipment.

Ford hasn’t released prices for either piece of hardware, so we don’t yet know what a complete home installation will cost.

But pairing a sub-$30,000 electric truck with substantially cheaper home power equipment could make bidirectional charging a lot more appealing.

Making the hardware cheaper is one thing. Making sure utilities can handle thousands of EVs that send electricity back into homes and potentially the grid is another.

Ford formed a working group in July with American Electric Power, BC Hydro, Consumers Energy, Exelon, and Pacific Gas and Electric. They’re working on making it easier for customers to connect bidirectional EVs before the Fathom arrives next year.

For example, someone using their truck solely for home backup power during an outage shouldn’t have to go through the same approval process as someone sending electricity to the grid.

The group is also looking at how to update utility procedures to accommodate newer bidirectional charging standards and make it easier for EV owners to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs). In other words, the batteries in parked EVs could become a useful source of electricity when the grid needs it most.

Ford says the Fathom’s system is designed to meet applicable UL 1741 requirements and IEEE 1547 interconnection standards. It also uses SAE J3068 communications technology, which Ford says helps reduce charger costs.

The idea is to get the technical requirements and utility processes sorted out before affordable bidirectional EVs start arriving in much larger numbers.

Affordable EVs already offer some form of bidirectional power. Two of the cheapest electric cars in the US, the Chevy Bolt and Nissan Leaf, are both available for under $30,000.

The Bolt supports vehicle-to-home (V2H) power through GM Energy equipment, while the Leaf offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capability through an external device plugged into its charging port.

Ford’s system takes things much further. It can deliver more than 10 kW of AC power to a home without an expensive external inverter, and Ford says the rest of the equipment will cost considerably less, too.

That’s a pretty compelling proposition, especially for people who live in areas prone to power outages or have electricity plans with higher peak-hour rates.

When power outages last a while the area still affected shrinks. While a whole county may be out day one, by day 3 it may just be your neighborhood left. At that point you could drive across town and recharge the car and be good to power your house for another few days.

There are still some unknowns. Ford hasn’t announced the final hardware prices, and installation costs will vary. Plus, utility rules need to catch up if EV owners are going to take full advantage of bidirectional charging.

But this seems to be going in the right direction. If automakers can bring costs down and the industry can agree on consistent standards, having an EV that doubles as a home battery could eventually become a normal part of EV ownership rather than an expensive bonus feature.

#4554. Rivian Has Invested Millions In 3D Printing. Its Biggest Plans Are Still Ahead

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Additive manufacturing is helping automakers come up with design mock-ups faster and cheaper than ever before, and Rivian is going all in on the technology. The California startup has spent over $5 million on 3D printers, using the machines to build tangible prototypes of various parts significantly faster than going down the traditional route, which involves at least one external supplier and big, expensive stamping equipment.

But Rivian is just getting started. In an interview with CNBC, Jonathan Dankenbring, the startup’s head of additive manufacturing, said that the company doesn’t have a choice but to scale up and begin using it across all factions. “We’re going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company,” Dankenbring said.

So far, the R2’s maker has used 3D printers on a relatively small scale at its facility in Detroit, Michigan. The R2’s steering wheel was first printed using additive manufacturing before becoming a metal part. The technology has also been used to make electric motors for fluid testing, screw guides for tooling, stamping press inserts, and some production parts, like trim pieces, for early builds.

For the next step, Rivian is installing new 3D printers that can build flexible silicone parts. At its factory in Normal, Illinois, where its entire lineup is being assembled, the startup is adding a bay of machines, enabling employees to print parts on demand. “3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible,” said Dankenbring for CNBC.

Besides the $5 million spent on 3D printers, Rivian is also paying roughly $1.7 million for the raw materials used in the machines every year. That’s quite a big sum for something that may look like big toys, but in the end, it makes a lot of financial sense for the EV manufacturer. According to Dankenbring, the cost savings have been “well in the millions” compared to traditional prototyping techniques, but more importantly, 3D printing speeds things up considerably.

By building small batches of parts on-site, the car company can lower its supplier tooling costs, cut logistics expenses, and reduce production times from weeks to days, and sometimes hours.

Rivian isn’t the only car manufacturer that has leaned into additive manufacturing. Tesla, Ford, General Motors, and many others have been using the technology to make stuff faster and cheaper, thanks in large part to the 3D printing industry’s massive advancements.

A decade ago, getting a 3D printer came with an eye-watering bill, but now, anyone can buy a machine for as little as a couple hundred dollars. The printers have also gotten smaller, faster, and more precise, enabling hobbyists and big companies to create bespoke parts in a matter of hours.

Correction: CNBC interviewed Jonathan Dankenbring, not Jared Beck. The article has been updated to reflect this change.

#4553. Ford Recalls 102,159 F-150 and Super Duty Trucks over Faulty Gauges

The trucks have been recalled due to malfunctioning analog gauges that could show incorrect speed readings.

Ford is recalling 102,159 F-150 and Super Duty trucks due to analog gauge clusters that could display incorrect speedometer and tachometer information. The automaker’s Super Duty lineup is most affected, with 91,588 F-250, F-350, F-450, F-550, and F-600 vehicles involved in the recall, all from the 2025–2026 model years. F-150s are also affected, but much less so, with just 10,570 units from the 2026 model year included. One 2026 F-750 has also been recalled.

Documents filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) say that analog tachometers and speedometers in the vehicles could get stuck or move erratically, which would show an inaccurate speed reading. No warning lights will appear in affected vehicles, but those with both digital and analog speedometers may see differences between the two readings.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405

Ford hasn’t received any accident reports, but the automaker identified 18 warranty and 93 field reports related to the issue by September 16. The affected vehicles aren’t produced in VIN order, so the best way to check a vehicle’s recall status, aside from waiting for an owner notification, is to call Ford’s hotline or contact a Ford or Lincoln dealer.

Owners of affected vehicles will be notified by October 30, but the replacement part won’t be ready until early December. Ford expects to alert owners of the available remedy by December 11. Once the new part is available, a dealer will replace the instrument cluster at no charge to the owner.

#4552. BYD names its ultra-luxury EV, and it could be a game changer next week

BYD’s new flagship EV will be its largest and most luxurious electric sedan yet, potentially debuting two firsts for the company next week: Rolls-Royce-style coach doors and solid-state batteries.

BYD is better known for its low-cost electric cars, like the Seagull, a little hatchback that sells for under $10,000 in China.

The Chinese auto giant has greatly expanded its portfolio over the past few months and years. BYD now offers everything from entry-level EVs to three-row flagship SUVs, pickup trucks, electric supercars, and just about everything in between.

BYD has three sub-brands: Denza, FangChengBao, and Yangwang. It also has two main families under the BYD brand: the Dynasty and Ocean series.

Yangwang sits at the top of BYD’s brand hierarchy and showcases its latest breakthrough technologies.

Previously, Yangwang vehicles debuted on BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering a whopping 1,300 horsepower and featuring its DiSus-X intelligent body control system, which enables the vehicle to “dance,” jump, and drive on three wheels.

For its next model, BYD is pushing further into the elite segment to take on ultra-luxury brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Maybach.

BYD revealed the name of its flagship ultra-luxury EV for the first time on Tuesday: the Yangwang Altior, along with a new teaser of the partially uncovered executive sedan.

Coming soon#YANGWANG #YANGWANGALTIOR pic.twitter.com/kFnu6X6csq

Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing said the name was chosen as an independent Chinese-English naming scheme. In China, it goes by DingYao. The “Ding” symbolizes stability and endurance, while “Yao” signifies radiant brilliance, or shining brightly like a star in the sky.

The English name Altior comes from Latin for “higher,” representing Yangwang’s relentless pursuit of ever-greater heights.

The new teaser comes after Hu revealed several images of the new Yangwang executive sedan testing for the first time last month.

Although it was disguised, it appeared to be about the same shape and size as the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom. Local reports indicate it will be around 5,500 mm (216″) long.

HU confirmed for the first time last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China.

BYD has not yet revealed a specific launch date, but the Yangwang sedan could make its first appearance as early as next week. According to CarNewsChina, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD is aiming to reveal the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5.

Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said the new model will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” but didn’t reveal specifics.

Although details are still limited, the ultra-luxury sedan was shown at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it will support megawatt flash charging.

It also features rear-hinged coach doors, a first for BYD. The flagship EV will reportedly be the first to feature BYD’s solid-state batteries.

BYD executive vice president Stella Li said during an interview with Carwow.es last month that the company’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027.

Li said BYD is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery technology and its commercialization, and the company plans to prove it next year.

BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, plans to begin production of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in 2027. It will initially be produced in limited batches, then scale to mass production closer to the end of the decade.

The part about solid state batteries got my attention. I'm looking forward to learning more about how they perform!

While BYD has yet to confirm it, introducing the new battery tech in a flagship model would make sense.

The executive sedan is expected to debut around November 5. Prices are rumored to start in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000.

Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The brand also sells the U8 (and U8L), a plug-in hybrid luxury off-road SUV, and the U9, a fully electric super-coupe.

The extended U8L is Yangwang’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

#4551. Arc Raiders' new map will be unlocked through a community event that starts today, and everyone has to donate

It looks like it's going to take the Arc Raiders community a bit of work to unlock the game's next map.

As many of Arc Raiders’ regular players predicted, the game’s first post-launch map won’t just be available for everyone, it will instead be closely tied to a community event. Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

The event kicks off today alongside the release of the game’s latest patch. The ask is relatively simple: players must commit Basic Materials to the project so that the tunnels can be rebuilt. This option will be available to anyone who’s played at least five rounds.

If you’ve spent any time in Arc Raiders, you’ll know that Basic Materials are things like Metal parts, Fabric, Chemicals, Rubber Parts, and Plastic Parts - most of which are easy to find in the game’s various maps.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the new map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a new progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

Developer Embark describes the new environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the new map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The update will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap update will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

#4550. Hyundai Says Hydrogen Cars Aren’t Dead. Finding Customers Is Another Story

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Hydrogen fuel cell cars were supposed to be the next leap forward in the automotive world. They drive like electric cars, but you can refuel them with hydrogen and drive hundreds of miles without having to sit at a charger for half an hour, and best of all, there are no nasty emissions.

It sounds like the perfect solution for pretty much everybody. Yet, ask anyone if they know someone who’s driving a hydrogen car, and they’ll struggle to come up with an answer. Toyota tried (and is still trying) with the Mirai, and Hyundai is still trying with the new Nexo. BMW, General Motors, Honda, and others have also dipped their toes into the technology, with varying degrees of success.

The second-generation Hyundai Nexo FCEV was unveiled in 2025, when it was touted as a global model.

But why aren’t we all driving FCEVs? For starters, there’s barely any hydrogen refueling infrastructure in place, and now a Hyundai executive has revealed that people don’t really want to buy a hydrogen car in the first place.

“The biggest thing is you’ve got to find customers, said Scott Nargar, Senior Manager of Future Mobility & Government Relations at Hyundai Australia, for CarExpert. Despite having problems finding buyers, the Hyundai representative insisted that hydrogen isn’t “dead for passenger vehicles.”

Besides having extremely limited access to refueling stations, hydrogen-powered cars are also more expensive than comparable gas and electric vehicles. That’s not exactly a good look, especially now when prices of new EVs are considerably lower than a decade ago, making them a perfect fit for those who are prepared to make the switch to electric.

What’s more, the electric charging infrastructure is now very well laid out, with even more chargers coming in the near future, making range anxiety and charging anxiety a thing of the past.

So with such easy access to electric cars, why would any company still bother to invest in hydrogen fuel cell vehicles? It all has to do with diversifying. In spite of the huge costs associated with developing a new fuel cell stack and installing refueling stations, some automakers, including Hyundai, believe that hydrogen will still have a place in the future where gas and diesel might not be as ubiquitous as they are today.

While Toyota decided to let anyone in California spend their hard-earned money to buy a Mirai, Hyundai’s hydrogen-fueled dream has been largely limited to a few real-world trials. Its latest passenger FCEV, the second-generation Nexo crossover, can drive roughly 435 miles on a full tank of hydrogen, powered by a 110-kilowatt electric motor and a 2.64-kilowatt-hour high-voltage battery that acts as a buffer between the motor and hydrogen fuel stack.

#4549. Musk declares Tesla Robotaxi win over Waymo, but Waymo still drives 7x more

Elon Musk says Tesla’s Robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest” after Tesla’s driverless fleet logged 438,000 miles in Austin in a single week, edging past Waymo’s 406,000 weekly average in the city.

That’s one city, one week, and a Waymo figure that’s four months old. Across the US, Waymo still drives about seven times more driverless miles than Tesla every week.

The chart going around comes from Robotaxi Tracker, a community project that pulls driverless mileage from each company’s own reports: Tesla’s weekly Robotaxi safety report and Waymo’s quarterly Safety Impact data hub.

Jason Scharf posted the Austin view on X with the comment that “the battle for Autonomous Austin might already be over.” Musk replied overnight: “It was never a real contest.”

The Austin data is real –albeit with some caveats. In the week ending October 18, Tesla reported 438,000 miles with no safety monitor aboard in Austin, up 30% from the week before. Waymo averaged about 406,000 miles a week in Austin in the second quarter.

But the tracker’s own caption explains the catch. Tesla’s figure is its latest week. Waymo’s is an average of April through June, because Waymo publishes about three months after each quarter ends. So Musk is comparing Tesla’s best week ever to Waymo’s spring.

Switch the same chart to “All markets” and the story flips.

Waymo averaged 3.90 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026. Tesla did 558,000 miles in its best week. Waymo’s Phoenix, Bay Area, and Los Angeles markets each drive more miles per week on their own than Tesla’s entire network.

Cumulative numbers are even more lopsided. Waymo has logged 271.3 million rider-only miles since 2020, including 50.7 million in Q2 alone, as we covered when Waymo released its latest safety data. Tesla has 3.11 million driverless miles since January 22, 2026. Waymo drove more than that in a single week.

And Tesla’s total leans almost entirely on one city:

Austin accounts for 79% of Tesla’s weekly driverless miles. Houston, Tampa, Orlando, and Miami combined did about 25,000 miles. Waymo’s smallest tracked market, Atlanta, averaged 250,000 a week in Q2.

The Austin surge has an obvious cause. Tesla launched public Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3.

According to Robotaxi Tracker’s count of the Texas DMV automated-vehicle list, Tesla now has 463 Cybercabs registered in Texas, 337 of them added in the last 30 days. That’s 48% of the 970 autonomous vehicles Tesla has registered in the state.

Tesla isn’t hiding the strategy. On the Q3 earnings call last week, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI software, said the company wants to “swarm Austin with Cybercabs everywhere.” Musk said the Austin Cybercab fleet had grown “by a factor of 10” in about a month.

So Tesla dumped hundreds of new, company-owned cars into one metro and the miles went up. That’s fleet deployment. It doesn’t show the software can do what Waymo does in 15 cities, and Tesla can’t repeat it everywhere at once.

The bigger problem is what the cars are allowed to do.

On the same earnings call, Elluswamy described the service as constrained by the software, not by regulators. He said that if there’s “the slightest possible risk at all,” Tesla doesn’t take it on, and that the limits are “technology driven” for now. Service hours only recently stretched from 9 p.m. toward 2 a.m., and he listed highways, “higher speed roads,” 24/7 operation, and more weather conditions as things Tesla still has to unlock.

You can see those limits in the rides. Tesla Robotaxis don’t take highways, and riders report they avoid at-grade railroad crossings. In September, a rider had a 10-minute Cybercab trip in Austin turn into a 70-minute detour because the car drove south through East Austin until it found a bridge over the rail line, instead of taking MoPac.

That matters for this comparison, too. Miles is a flattering metric when your car takes the long way. A trip that should cover a few miles and instead loops across town logs a lot more mileage for the same rider.

Waymo, meanwhile, has been taking riders on freeways in Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles since November 2025.

Credit where it’s due: Tesla’s driverless miles are growing fast, 30% in a single week, and Austin now has a real Tesla fleet carrying the public without anyone in the driver’s seat. A year ago, that wasn’t the case.

#4548. Smart’s New City EV Is Already Off To A Great Start

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The Smart car had a pretty short life in the United States, especially when it comes to the two-door electric model. However, over in Europe, the two-door urban runabout has become something of an icon, and can often be seen in the busy streets of major cities.

Now, though, there’s a new two-door Smart EV, which harks back to the original ForTwo EQ, but significantly improves on its predecessor’s spec sheet. And to the company’s surprise, the first batch of the new Smart #2 is also proving quite successful, with order books already full.

I’m talking about the limited-run Smart #2 Couture Edition, which kicked off sales of the diminutive EV in Europe. Limited to just 999 units, the two-tone version of the bug-eyed city car is already sold out in all of the countries where it was available, signaling that Europeans are interested in Smart’s modern reinterpretation of the car that started it all.

To be clear, the Smart #2 in its regular trims can still be ordered and probably won’t be sold out anytime soon. But for a car that can only seat two and has a WLTP-rated range of just 180 miles (290 kilometers), it’s a pretty solid start.

The #2 Couture Edition is based on the top Premium trim and comes standard with a glass roof, ambient lighting, heated seats, a heated steering wheel, a Sennheiser audio system, and a wireless charging pad for smartphones. On top of that, the exterior is painted in an exclusive Atelier White Matt color with a Platinum Gold roof. Together with the 16-inch Lyra rims with gold details and suitcase-like straps in the front bumper, the limited edition model is meant to look like the Smart Concept #2 that prefaced the model’s introduction half a year ago.

“Selling out all currently available units of the Smart #2 Couture Edition in just two weeks is an extraordinary achievement,” said Wolfgang Ufer, CEO of Smart Europe GmbH. “And what makes this success even more remarkable is that most of our customers haven't even had the chance to see the car in person yet. For me, this is much more than a sales success. It's a powerful sign of how much people have been waiting for the return of our iconic two-seater.”

The successor to the Smart ForTwo EQ is powered by a 35.8-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, which is almost double the original model’s 17.6-kWh capacity. As a result, the range has also doubled. The charging performance has also been improved dramatically, with the new Smart #2 needing roughly 20 minutes to go from 10% to 80% state of charge.

In several European countries, including Germany, France, and Italy, the new EV starts at €19,990 ($22,500). The first customer deliveries in left-hand drive markets are scheduled for the middle of the second quarter, with right-hand drive markets following in 2027.

#4547. An Italian Company Is Building the Ultimate Ferrari 308 Tribute

The Gruppo Four Tributo builds on experience preparing Ferraris for tarmac and gravel racing and keeps the recipe delightfully simple.

Ferrari’s new 12Cilindri Manuale offers buyers a slightly ersatz version of the six-speed-manual Maranello V-12 grand tourers of the past, complete with a metallic gated gearshift. There’s a bit of electronic trickery going on behind the scenes, but we were pretty convinced by our test drive of the tech. However, a suggestion: What if the manual gearbox was real, and the Ferrari part was the tribute?

Say hello to the familiar shape of the iconic Ferrari 308 GTB, albeit one without a single Ferrari badge on it. Rather than being a restomodded version of the car that Magnum P.I. waggled his caterpillar-sized eyebrows in, it's a ground-up build by longtime Ferrari motorsports specialist Michelotto working in partnership with a newer firm, AC Motorsport, itself founded by a former Michelotto employee. It’s called the Michelotto Gruppo Four Tributo, and it’s a featherweight wonder.

See all results for used Ferrari for sale near 20147

Michelotto has more than half a century of experience taking already well-bred cavallino rampantes and getting them ready for the track. The company’s past hits include belters like the F40 LM, the competition version of Ferrari’s ultimate 1980s supercar. Michelotto also prepared the 308 for rally racing in Group 4 competition, eventually leading to Ferrari's sole WRC podium victory.

This road car pays homage to that rally car, but it is set up purely for tarmac work. The foundation starts with a tubeframe chassis with a built-in roll cage, upon which is layered that immediately recognizable wedge-shaped body, formed of carbon composite panels. There’s a bit of a parallel here with the original Ferrari F40, which was designed for the stillborn Group B racing series, then metamorphosed into a 200-mph supercar.

Rather than turbocharged power, the Gruppo Four Tributo is motivated by a naturally aspirated, all-aluminum 3.4-liter V-8. Peak power is 380 horsepower at 8250 rpm, fed through a five-speed dogleg manual gearbox. This is old-school Italian exotic; no six-speed manual, no hybrids, no turbochargers, just a sky-high redline and yes, pop-up headlights.

However, there’s nothing old-school about the carbon-fiber bodywork. Thanks to its composite construction and simple powertrain recipe, the Gruppo Four Tributo is claimed to tip the scales at just 2094 pounds. Time to slip on your favorite Nomex Hawaiian shirt.

As with most reinventions of heroic classics, prices are expected to be high and production levels low. However, given the $200,000 premium Ferrari is charging for the simulated-manual version of the 12Cilindri over the standard model, and taking into account Michelotto’s 55 years of motorsports heritage, the Gruppo Four Tributo might be the way to go for stick-shift Italian bliss.

#4545. How to Determine If Buying Out Your Car’s Lease Is Worth It

Calculating your lease buyout and understanding the associated costs are only parts of the equation.

If you’re nearing the end of your vehicle’s lease and unsure about your personal transportation plans after the lease is over, then a car lease buyout may be an option worth considering. Provided you really like the car you’re leasing and aren’t quite yet ready to return it.

Perhaps the car is in excellent condition and doesn’t require significant maintenance or repair services. Or maybe you’ve grown accustomed to its reliability and need long-term transportation. Alternatively, a lease buyout might make financial sense if the car’s residual value is less than the market value. Before you buy out your car lease, consider additional factors, such as timing and finances, to help you decide.

A lease buyout is when you purchase your leased vehicle before or when the lease term ends. To do this, you pay something known as the buyout cost.

The buyout cost is equal to the residual value the leasing company estimated the vehicle would be worth at the end of the lease term, along with any taxes, fees, and remaining lease payments due. Before you begin the lease buyout process, double-check your lease agreement to make sure this option is allowed.

See all results for used cars for sale near 21014

Understanding how a car lease buyout works and what to expect can help you make the right decision as you near the end of your car lease. Two lease buyout options determine when you can complete the process:

If a buyout option is available in your lease contract, this typically means you can purchase the vehicle at the end of the lease. You might consider a lease-end buyout option if you like your car and don’t want to hassle with starting a new lease or buying a new car. Instead of returning the car to the leasing company, you buy it and assume ownership.

You might also want to pursue a lease-end buyout when it makes financial sense. This is typically when the car’s market value is higher than what you’d have to pay to purchase it.

An early lease buyout involves purchasing the vehicle before your lease contract ends. This option is less common and can be expensive if your leasing company applies early termination fees on top of the car’s buyout price.

However, it might be your best option if you’re worried about excess wear and tear or mileage fees associated with your lease contract.

Here are some simple tips to follow to calculate your car lease buyout amount:

The car’s residual value is its expected worth at the end of your lease and accounts for the vehicle’s depreciation during the lease term. The leasing company determines this number, and you’ll be able to view it before signing the lease. Typically, your lease agreement states the residual value.

See all results for used cars for sale near 21014

The market value of your vehicle is the amount of money a dealership or buyer would pay for it. Use the Car and Driver car value calculator to determine your vehicle’s worth based on its location, make and model, age, current condition, features, and mileage.

Comparing your vehicle’s residual value and current market value can clarify whether it makes financial sense to buy out the lease. Remember that leasing companies usually don’t negotiate the residual value, which is a major part of the buyout price. So if your car is worth less than the residual value stated in your contract, buying out the lease may not make financial sense.

Depending on your location, you may have to pay local and/or state used car sales taxes as part of the buyout cost. Plan to pay extra for licensing or registration fees for registering a new vehicle under your name, too.

Some leasing companies charge a purchase option fee, and the buyout price can also include remaining lease payments, especially for an early buyout. Double-check your lease agreement so you’re prepared for additional costs.

If the lease buyout option is available in your contract, you can tell the leasing company of your purchase intentions at the appropriate time. You could seek a lease buyout loan from a financial institution to finance the purchase.

A lease buyout loan is similar to an auto loan in which you have set monthly payments, an annual interest rate, and a set loan term or specified loan length. Of course, if you have funds set aside to purchase a vehicle, you can opt to take care of the buyout fee in cash.

Are you prepared to purchase your leased vehicle? If so, we suggest conducting some independent research to help determine if a lease buyout is right for you. If you still have questions, consider the following factors:

It’s important to consider the timing of your car lease buyout. Let’s say you want to buy your leased car a year before your lease ends. In this case, you should check your lease contract to see if you’d be subject to any additional fees associated with ending your car lease early. If you are, it might be best to wait until the lease ends before buying out your lease.

Determining your car’s current value can help you decide if it’s worth purchasing. Look up the retail price of your car, which is what you would pay a car dealership to buy it. Next, try to find out the vehicle’s wholesale value, or the price a dealer might pay to buy the car at an auction.

Compare these amounts with the vehicle’s residual value. Buying the car might be a good idea if the market value is higher than the residual value. If the opposite is true, the car is likely not worth purchasing.

It’s normal to require financing for your car lease buyout. Your current leasing company might offer financing options, though you aren’t obligated to stick with it.

Contact other finance companies, such as banks or credit unions, to check what kind of loans they offer. Some service providers offer competitive rates, but you won’t know until you shop around.

Having good credit can also improve your chances of getting a better deal. Keep in mind that the higher your credit score, the more likely a lender is to offer you a lower interest rate on your lease buyout loan.

Many leasing companies have a non-negotiation clause in their lease agreement, meaning you can’t negotiate the buyout price. Regardless, it doesn’t hurt to ask the question.

Some lessors are willing to negotiate and might offer financing discounts or purchase incentives. You could also get the potential purchase option fee waived if you try to negotiate.

It’s customary for your leasing company to contact you within 90 days before your lease expires. Try to wait for it to make the first move and contact you about the lease ending.

Doing so gives you the upper hand when expressing your desire to purchase the leased vehicle. It could also make the lessor more open to negotiations versus letting it know your intentions early.

Buying out a car lease isn’t for everyone, especially if it doesn’t make financial sense. What if the car’s buyout price is higher than its market value? For example, if a car's buyout price is $10,000, but it’s only worth $7500, it might be better to trade the vehicle for a new lease, as purchasing it wouldn’t make financial sense.

In contrast, a car lease buyout may be worthwhile if the vehicle’s market value exceeds the buyout price. You should ensure that a lease buyout makes sense for you financially. However, if you feel strongly about purchasing your car because you’ve grown attached to it, you might consider buying it even if the buyout cost exceeds the market value.

Read your lease terms to understand your lease buyout eligibility and the potential fees involved. Remember to consider the timing and financing factors versus the value and condition of your leased car. You can proceed with buying out the lease if it’s worth it.

#4544. Korean police book 80 Tesla drivers over illegal FSD unlock devices

Seoul police have booked 80 people for using aftermarket devices to switch on Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” in cars that aren’t allowed to run it in South Korea. Officers also seized 21 of the devices.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency announced the case on Tuesday. It’s the largest enforcement action yet against the FSD “jailbreak” hardware that has spread through China, Europe, and Korea over the past year.

Police say the suspects either imported the unlock modules from Europe and China or made their own. One plugged a European-made unit into his own Tesla. Another, an IT worker, built his device with information he found on GitHub.

Suspects also swapped advice online on how to unlock FSD and how to stop the car from keeping any record that it had been activated.

They’re charged under Korea’s Motor Vehicle Management Act, which bans unauthorized software changes that can affect a vehicle’s safety. The penalty is up to two years in prison or a fine of up to 20 million won (about $15,000).

The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport asked police to look into it back in April after finding signs of unauthorized activation. A police official told Korea JoongAng Daily that “safety risks were confirmed,” including the possibility of FSD misreading driving conditions. The investigation is ongoing, with police consulting the ministry and the Korea Transportation Safety Authority on the technical side.

Tesla launched FSD (Supervised) in South Korea in late 2025, but only on US-built vehicles: Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck. Those cars are exempt from Korean safety certification under the Korea-US free trade agreement. The Model 3 and Model Y, which Tesla ships to Korea from Giga Shanghai, haven’t cleared Korea’s safety standards for the feature.

And those two models are the bulk of the fleet. Citing Carisyou Data Lab, Korea JoongAng Daily reports that 47,458 of the 229,311 Teslas on Korean roads as of August, or 20.7%, can legally use FSD.

That number doesn’t match the government’s own count from a few months earlier. In May, data released by lawmaker Park Yong-gap showed just 4,292 of 180,684 registered Teslas (2.4%) were eligible: 2,708 Model X, 1,193 Model S, and 391 Cybertruck. Either way, the vast majority of Korean Tesla owners can’t legally use FSD, and some of them paid over $6,000 for it anyway.

The hardware is the same, which is why the hack works. The modules plug into the car’s CAN bus and get around the regional software lock.

Tesla has been fighting the devices itself. In April, it started remotely detecting them and stripping FSD from affected cars, warned owners they’d be fully liable for any crash and could lose warranty coverage, and permanently banned some Chinese owners from FSD.

It was that year that a programming glitch came where some vehicles would not function. That was quickly corrected. In the news today where proof that when Elon shut down Starlink to Ukraine, russian missiles came and killed 5 people, including one baby. ... here is the reality you and me must face: Musk holds the power right now, that if he decides he does not like 'some owners' of Teslas, he can SHUT DOWN instantly those vehicles from moving. It is not enough that potentially, every conversation and communication device used inside those vehicles 'can' be recorded but, as he has proven perfectly willing to do to Ukraine families, so he could at any moment 'shut down' some specific users of Tesla vehicles at-will. this is not hype, fantasy or gusswork. This is how the online active update software communications system works on every car we buy from Tesla. My company is looking into other providers of Sat-Com services, and we are re-evaluating our own vehicle choices.

It’s easy to see why people do this. Picture a Korean owner of a Shanghai-built Model Y who paid for FSD, watching the Model X next door run the same software on the same computer. That’s frustrating.

Tesla sold FSD to owners of cars it had no regulatory path to enable in Korea, the same way it sold “Full Self-Driving” in Europe for years while approval kept slipping. It only dropped the name there this month after Germany pushed back. Sell a feature people can’t legally use and you create the market for the jailbreak.

Korea has now shown it will actually prosecute. So will Tesla refund the Korean owners who bought a feature their cars may never be allowed to run?
